_disclaimer: Pre-defined protocol cards for the Medical Assistant in the BAYOU-NOVA proof of concept (2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge). Fixed text, written in advance from the published sources named on each card. NOT generated by an AI model. NOT reviewed by a clinician. Not for clinical use.
required_line: Contact your flight surgeon at the next available communication window. Do not wait for symptoms to resolve.
onboard_line: Tell your crew medical officer or a crewmate now. Do not manage this alone.
fixed_text_note: This card is fixed text written in advance from the sources named on it. It is not generated by an AI model, and nothing in your readings or your personal baseline can change it.
clinical_review: PENDING. No flight surgeon has reviewed this card. Your mission's own onboard medical procedures and your flight surgeon's instructions always take priority over it.
sourcing_finding: NASA's International Space Station emergency medical procedures are only partly public. The released set (FOIA 16-JSC-F-00174) covers severe allergic reaction, CPR, advanced life support, choking, toxic exposure, seizure and difficulty breathing. No published spaceflight emergency procedure was found for chest pain, stroke signs, sudden severe headache, sudden vision loss, new confusion or a psychological crisis. For those, each card follows the published guideline written for people on Earth that Layer 1 already cites, adds what NASA's own planning documents say, and says so on the card.
visitor_note: BAYOU-NOVA is a demonstration that runs on simulated data. If you are a visitor and this is about you, in real life, please contact your local emergency number or a crisis line in your country now.

protocols.title: Chest pain or pressure, or a racing or irregular heartbeat with other symptoms
protocols.follows_note: Gulati et al. 2021 and the American Heart Association warning signs were written for people on Earth, where the instruction is to call emergency services at once. The ground-contact step follows the International Space Station emergency medical procedures.
protocols.spaceflight_gap: No published spaceflight emergency procedure for chest pain was found. The steps on this card are the published guidance for Earth, with the mission equivalent of each stated.

steps.text: Stop what you are doing.

Get help straight away, even if you are not sure what it is. On Earth the published instruction is to call emergency services at the first warning sign and not to wait. On a mission that means your crew medical officer now, and mission control.

Ask mission control for a private medical conference with your flight surgeon. The released International Space Station emergency procedures end their assessment with the step "Call MCC-H to request PMC".

Note when it started, what it feels like, where it spreads, and anything that came with it: shortness of breath, cold sweat, nausea, light-headedness, a rapid or irregular heartbeat. These are the published warning signs your flight surgeon will ask about.

Expect the ground to be involved in working out what this is. NASA's planning document for acute coronary syndrome considered ground communication necessary during diagnosis, which in that plan uses a troponin blood test, an ECG and ultrasound.

If a crew member collapses or stops responding, the crew's own resuscitation procedure applies. The published guideline for CPR in microgravity says telemedicine support should be consulted when that is feasible.

protocols.cannot: BAYOU-NOVA cannot record an ECG, measure troponin or examine you. A wearable resting heart rate is not a heart rhythm. It cannot tell what is causing this.

protocols.title: Severe or unexplained shortness of breath
protocols.follows_note: International Space Station emergency medical procedure 1.108 Difficulty Breathing, dated 20 April 2015, as released under FOIA 16-JSC-F-00174. Its stated objective is "To evaluate and start treatment for difficulty breathing."
protocols.spaceflight_gap: This is the one red flag for which a published spaceflight emergency procedure was found. It may have been revised since 2015. The card summarises it; it does not replace the procedure on board.

steps.text: Tell your crew medical officer now and open your onboard Difficulty Breathing procedure. Follow that procedure in its own order. Its treatment steps (oxygen and medication) are for the crew medical officer and the onboard kit, and are not reproduced here.
The procedure has the crew measure and write down, for the flight surgeon: pulse, breathing rate, blood oxygen saturation from the oximeter, and blood pressure.
It then has the crew look at the mouth, nose, neck and chest, listen to both lungs, and take a history: when it started, medication, any fever or cough, and how severe the breathing difficulty is.
It ends with the step "Call MCC-H to request PMC": ask mission control for a private medical conference with your flight surgeon.
Shortness of breath, with or without chest discomfort, is also a published heart attack warning sign. Say so if there is any chest discomfort, cold sweat, nausea or light-headedness.

protocols.cannot: BAYOU-NOVA does not measure breathing rate or blood oxygen and cannot listen to your lungs. It cannot see cabin air quality.

protocols.title: Fainting or nearly fainting
protocols.follows_note: Shen et al. 2017 and Brignole et al. 2018 were written for people on Earth. The ground-contact step follows the International Space Station emergency medical procedures.
protocols.spaceflight_gap: No published spaceflight emergency procedure for fainting was found. The Earth guidelines assume gravity; fainting on standing is not expected in microgravity, which makes an episode in flight harder, not easier, to explain.

steps.text: Stop what you are doing and tell your crew medical officer or a crewmate now.
Both published guidelines call for prompt medical evaluation of fainting. On a mission that means asking mission control for a private medical conference with your flight surgeon.
Note what you were doing when it happened. Fainting during exertion, or with a racing or irregular heartbeat just before it, is a published high-risk feature, so say if either applies.
If chest discomfort or breathlessness came with it, say so. Each is a red flag in its own right.

protocols.cannot: BAYOU-NOVA cannot record an ECG or check blood pressure at the moment of an episode, and it cannot tell why it happened.

protocols.title: Sudden vision loss, weakness, numbness, speech difficulty, confusion or loss of balance
protocols.follows_note: American Stroke Association stroke warning signs and BE-FAST (Aroor et al. 2017) were written for people on Earth, where the instruction is to call emergency services at once. The ground-contact step follows the International Space Station emergency medical procedures.
protocols.spaceflight_gap: No published spaceflight emergency procedure for stroke signs was found. Disorientation and motion sickness are common while adapting to microgravity, so loss of balance is less specific in flight than on Earth. It is still treated as a red flag here; the flight surgeon decides what it means.

steps.text: Treat this as an emergency. The published guidance is that every minute counts. Tell your crew medical officer or a crewmate now.
Note the time the first symptom appeared. This is the first thing a clinician will ask.

Ask a crewmate to check what the published warning-sign list checks: ask you to smile and see whether one side of the face droops, ask you to raise both arms and see whether one drifts down, and listen for slurred or strange speech.
Act even if the symptom goes away. The published guidance is to seek help even when symptoms stop.

Ask mission control for a private medical conference with your flight surgeon. NASA's planning document for stroke notes that CT and MRI are unavailable in flight, so the assessment rests on history and examination, and considered communication with ground specialists necessary.

protocols.cannot: BAYOU-NOVA cannot examine you and cannot tell a stroke from any other cause. Gradual vision change is a separate question: spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS) is under active investigation and this platform cannot assess it.

protocols.title: Sudden, severe headache
protocols.follows_note: The SNNOOP10 red-flag list (Do et al. 2019), the Ottawa Subarachnoid Hemorrhage Rule (Perry et al. 2013) and the American Stroke Association warning signs were written for people on Earth. The ground-contact step follows the International Space Station emergency medical procedures.
protocols.spaceflight_gap: No published spaceflight emergency procedure for sudden severe headache was found. Headache is common in spaceflight, but a sudden or severe one is a published red flag wherever it happens.

steps.text: Tell your crew medical officer or a crewmate now. A severe headache with no known cause is a published stroke warning sign, and sudden onset is a published red flag for a serious cause.
Note the time it started and how fast it reached its worst. A headache that peaks at once is the "thunderclap" feature in the published decision rule.
Tell your flight surgeon whether any of these came with it, because the published rule asks about each: neck pain or stiffness, any loss of consciousness, and whether it began during exertion.
Say at once if there is also any change in vision, weakness, numbness, trouble speaking or confusion. A headache with a neurological change is a published red flag in its own right.
Ask mission control for a private medical conference with your flight surgeon.

protocols.cannot: BAYOU-NOVA cannot see cabin carbon dioxide, pressure inside the head or anything a scan would show. It cannot tell what is causing the headache.

protocols.title: Blood pressure above 180 systolic and/or 120 diastolic
protocols.follows_note: Whelton et al. 2018 (ACC/AHA high blood pressure guideline), Figure 11, written for people on Earth. The ground-contact step follows the International Space Station emergency medical procedures.
protocols.spaceflight_gap: No published spaceflight emergency procedure for a very high blood pressure reading was found.

steps.text: Report the reading to your crew medical officer now, with the time it was taken.
The guideline uses this value as its decision point for a hypertensive crisis. Whether it is an emergency depends on signs of organ damage, which only a clinician can assess.

Say at once if any of these is present, because each is a red flag in its own right: chest pain, shortness of breath, a change in vision, weakness or numbness, trouble speaking, confusion, or a severe headache.
Ask mission control for a private medical conference with your flight surgeon.

protocols.cannot: BAYOU-NOVA cannot check cuff fit, repeat the measurement for you, or assess organ damage.

protocols.title: Resting heart rate above 100 bpm
protocols.follows_note: Page et al. 2016 (ACC/AHA/HRS guideline), Table 3, written for people on Earth. The ground-contact step follows the International Space Station emergency medical procedures.
protocols.spaceflight_gap: No published spaceflight emergency procedure for a fast resting heart rate was found. Above 100 bpm at rest is the published definition of tachycardia. It is a definition, not by itself an emergency criterion; it sits in Layer 1 so that it is never explained away by a personal baseline.

steps.text: Report the reading to your crew medical officer now, with the time it was taken and what you were doing before it.
Say at once if any of these is present, because each is a red flag in its own right: chest discomfort, shortness of breath, light-headedness or fainting, or a pounding or irregular heartbeat.
Ask mission control for a private medical conference with your flight surgeon.

protocols.cannot: BAYOU-NOVA shows a wearable resting value, not an ECG. It cannot see heart rhythm, hydration, illness or medication.

protocols.title: Thoughts of being better off dead, or of hurting yourself
protocols.follows_note: Simon et al. 2013 and Kroenke et al. 2001 (PHQ-9 item 9) are general clinical sources written for people on Earth. Slack et al. 2016 is the NASA evidence report that defines a behavioural emergency in spaceflight.
protocols.spaceflight_gap: No published spaceflight criterion or procedure for thoughts of self-harm was found. NASA's planning documents note that the International Space Station medical checklist includes a Behavioral Emergency procedure; it is not public, so it cannot be reproduced here.

steps.text: Please tell someone now: your flight surgeon, your behavioural health provider or your crew medical officer, and a crewmate you trust. You do not have to manage this alone.

In a large published study, any answer above "not at all" to this question identified people at increased risk who needed clinical follow-up. That is why it is acted on here whatever else your data shows.

Ask mission control for a private conference with your flight surgeon or behavioural health provider. Private medical and psychological conferences are a standing part of mission support (NASA-STD-3001 requirements V1 6002 and V1 6010), and the released International Space Station emergency procedures show a private medical conference being requested through mission control.

protocols.cannot: BAYOU-NOVA cannot assess risk and is not a crisis service. It has told no one: nothing typed here is sent anywhere, so only you can make the contact.

protocols.title: Altered perception, being unable to function, or urges that could endanger others
protocols.follows_note: Slack et al. 2016 (NASA Human Research Program Evidence Report) defines a behavioural emergency in spaceflight; NASA's Behavioral Emergency Clinical Finding Form and technical brief OCHMO-TB-016 give the context. These are published space medicine sources, but none of them is a step-by-step crew procedure.
protocols.spaceflight_gap: NASA's planning document notes that the International Space Station medical checklist includes a Behavioral Emergency procedure. It is not public, so it cannot be reproduced here. "Urges that could endanger others" rests on documented cases, not a validated criterion.

steps.text: Please tell someone now: your flight surgeon, your behavioural health provider or your crew medical officer, and a crewmate you trust. You do not have to manage this alone.

NASA defines a behavioural emergency as any behavioural condition or psychiatric disorder that causes serious behavioural or cognitive symptoms leading to incapacitation. What you describe may be consistent with that definition, which is why it is acted on here whatever else your data shows.

Ask mission control for a private conference with your flight surgeon or behavioural health provider. Private medical and psychological conferences are a standing part of mission support (NASA-STD-3001 requirements V1 6002 and V1 6010), and the released International Space Station emergency procedures show a private medical conference being requested through mission control.
New confusion or disorientation can also be a sign of a physical problem. Say so if it is present; it is a red flag in its own right.

protocols.cannot: BAYOU-NOVA cannot assess your state of mind and is not a crisis service. It has told no one: nothing typed here is sent anywhere, so only you can make the contact.
